chapter: Last job, serenades and New Orleans venues
title: Venues and the carnival schedule; music-loving habits
summary: Places he played, a Mardi Gras schedule of parades and Antoine's, his crystal set, and his insistence on soft playing.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I think my brother put all this down. But I told you, you know, one place he played, I didn't tell you about, the Absinthe House. And that Jitney place you were talking about, I think that was... The Lovita? No, I think... He played at the Lovita. I know that. The Music Gods.
I know he played at the Lovita, because he used my trumpet when he played at the Lovita.
Well, he could use it. The Music Gods.
The Music Gods. Yeah, he played there, too. And the foreign name's home. He played at the Alamore. With the foreign, he used to play at the foreign, right?

And he played at Antoine's Restaurant? That's another place. In La Lusanne? La Lusanne, yeah. But you know what he did one time? In fact, that's what he used to do every year. They used to have the Rival King. That was on Monday. On Monday, about 1 o'clock. And they had a parade. So he'd play that parade that day.
Is that when the wrecks would come in on the river?

On the river. They'd go in with the king on the river. And they'd have that parade in the day. Then they'd have the parade at night. And he'd play that night parade. He'd leave the night. When the night parade was over, he'd go to Antoine's Restaurant. He'd play there. Then the next day, he'd play the day parade, which was carnival then. And he'd come home. Then he'd go back for the night parade. And when he'd leave the night parade, he'd go back to La Lusanne. Oh, yeah. And then it was Wednesday morning. He'd get in the bed. Then he couldn't get up the next day at all. No wonder. He was blown up. But you know, he was really a lover of music. He'd play all night on the job, coming around 2, 3 o'clock in the morning. And he had a little crystal set, radio set, with the feeler, you know. And he'd sit in a rocker and sit with that little set until sometimes 7 o'clock in the morning. After playing all night.

Just trying to find what he could on that little crystal. He never got tired of music. I don't understand. And then you could hear him to himself, that's a bottle man band. A what? Bottle man. You know the bottle man? Oh, yes. He couldn't stand blasting music. He told you that. He couldn't stand that. He'd come in and say, what's the matter now? He looks so aggravated. He said, oh, we had a rehearsal then. I can't make them fellas understand that they can blow loud and soft. And they're just aggravating. And he said, there's nothing to it. I said, well, there's nothing to it because you know. That's not, if they can't do it. It's true. So you could go up with a high, high note and it would never pierce your ears. Yet it was high. It was soft. Soft. We had to blow. So. We really had that gift of going like that. Oh, yes. Well, sometimes he'd be laying in the bed and she'd be practicing. And he'd tell, uh-uh. We thought he was sleeping. On the piano? Yeah. He said, uh-uh, that's not right. Go over it again. Then he'd get up. He couldn't stand it. He'd start playing the carnet with her. We played him many pieces together.
